## Content

::: {.toc-grid}
1 · The problem: NEET among young women

2 · Who is most affected

3 · From education to earnings

4 · The cost of inaction

5 · Investment options

6 · Conclusions and recommendations

Appendix
:::

## Data sources {.smaller}

- **Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) 2025/26**, State Statistics Service of Ukraine with UNICEF: 23,708 households, 37,315 household members, 8,213 women aged 15–49 selected for interview, and children 5–17. There is no men's questionnaire. Main source for education, NEET and employment among young women, marriage, motherhood, disability, displacement, wealth and changes in households since the beginning of the conflict.
- **UNICEF Household Social and Economic Status Survey (HSESS)**, December 2023 to February 2024, Institute of Demography and Quality of Life Problems: 18,838 individuals in 8,024 households, all regions covered by the survey (Luhansk oblast is not included). Covers women and men: participation, employment, NEET, job quality, occupations, earnings and childcare.
- **SSSU Labour Force Survey 2021** (anonymised public-use file), collected in 2021: 265.6k interviews from 151.7k persons aged 15+. Shown for reference only.

# 1 · The problem {.section-divider background-color="#00377C"}

## `r MH("neet_w_1824")`% of women aged 18–24 are NEET {.smaller}
```{r q1, results='asis'}
FIG("m2b_neet_women_by_age_en.png", "62%")
```

::: {style="font-size:0.58em; color:#7a7a7a;"}
MICS 2025/26. NEET: not in education or training and not employed. At 15–17 the rate is `r MH("neet_w_1518")`%: almost all girls are still in education. The survey asks these questions to women from age 15, so NEET cannot be measured at 14.
:::

## The gap with young men comes from education, not employment {.smaller}
```{r q2, results='asis'}
FIG("h19b_neet_waterfall_en.png", "84%")
```

::: {style="font-size:0.58em; color:#7a7a7a;"}
HSESS 2023/24, ages 18–24. NEET: women `r HS("st_neet_w")`%, men `r HS("st_neet_m")`%. In education: women `r HS("st_educ_w")`%, men `r HS("st_educ_m")`%. Employed and not in education: women `r HS("st_emp_w")`%, men `r HS("st_emp_m")`%. NEET is what remains after education and employment.
:::

## At 14–17, almost all girls and boys are in school {.smaller}
```{r q3, results='asis'}
FIG("m1_attendance_by_level_en.png", "84%")
```

::: {style="font-size:0.58em; color:#7a7a7a;"}
MICS 2025/26, household members attending in the current school year. Ages 14–17: girls `r MH("att_w_1417")`%, boys `r MH("att_m_1417")`%. Ages 18–24: women `r MH("att_w_1824")`%, men `r MH("att_m_1824")`%. School attendance is available from age 14; NEET and employment only from age 15. MICS does not show the gap in education at 18–24 that HSESS shows; the surveys differ in date, respondent and definition.
:::

# 3 · From education to earnings {.section-divider background-color="#00377C"}

## NEET falls with education {.smaller}
```{r q8, results='asis'}
FIG("h13_outcomes_by_education_en.png", "96%")
```

::: {style="font-size:0.58em; color:#7a7a7a;"}
HSESS 2023/24, ages 18–24, by highest level completed. NEET among women: `r HS("neet_w_higher")`% with higher education, `r HS("neet_w_sec")`% with complete secondary. Many 18–24 year olds are still studying, so rates by level should be read together with the share in education.
:::

## No significant NEET gap between vocational and secondary education {.smaller}
```{r g7, results='asis'}
FIG("g7_vet_effect_controls_en.png", "78%")
```

::: {style="font-size:0.58em; color:#7a7a7a;"}
HSESS 2023/24, women aged 18–29. Each dot is a regression coefficient: the difference in the NEET rate between women with vocational and with complete secondary education (linear probability model, oblast fixed effects), with its 95% confidence interval, as controls are added. The difference is `r GH("g7_raw")` pp without controls and `r GH("g7_full")` pp with all controls; no interval excludes zero, so the difference is not statistically significant in any specification. NEET by level: vocational `r GH("vet_neet_w")`%, complete secondary `r GH("sec_neet_w")`%, tertiary `r GH("tert_neet_w")`%.
:::

## Women earn less than men at every level of education {.smaller}
```{r q8c, results='asis'}
FIG("h20_mincer_by_education_en.png", "82%")
```

::: {style="font-size:0.58em; color:#7a7a7a;"}
HSESS 2023/24, wage earners aged 18–64. Predicted net monthly wage at age 30 in an urban area. Gap at comparable age and area: `r MM("gap_sec_adj", 0)`% with complete secondary, `r MM("gap_higher_adj", 0)`% with higher education. Each additional year of education is associated with `r MM("ret_w")`% higher wages for women and `r MM("ret_m")`% for men. Not adjusted for hours, occupation or sector.
:::

# 4 · The cost of inaction {.section-divider background-color="#00377C"}

## How the cost of inaction is calculated {.smaller}

::: {.kv-table}
| Step | What is used | Source |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Who** | NEET women aged 18–24: `r CH("neet_w", 1)`% of young women, about `r CHK("n_neet_nat")` in the areas covered by the survey | MICS 2025/26; HSESS 2023/24 weights |
| **2. What they could earn** | Wage predicted for each NEET young woman from her education, age and place of residence, using a wage equation estimated on employed women: UAH `r CH("wage_cent")` a month on average | HSESS 2023/24 |
| **3. How many could work** | Pessimistic: `r tolower(.sct$Basis[1])` (`r CH("avoid_pess")`%). Central: `r tolower(.sct$Basis[2])` (`r CH("avoid_cent")`%). Optimistic: `r tolower(.sct$Basis[3])` (`r CH("avoid_opt")`%) | HSESS 2023/24 |
| **4. How many jobs are formal** | `r CH("formal_pess")`% to `r CH("formal_opt")`%: formal share among employed young women, by level of education | HSESS 2023/24 |
| **5. Who gains** | Young women (net earnings) and the budget (income tax, military levy, employer social contribution, VAT) | Statutory rates |
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.56em; color:#7a7a7a;"}
The cost of inaction is what is forgone each year that these young women remain NEET. Results are shown for the country and per 1,000 NEET young women (about `r CH("young_per1000")` women aged 18–24). Full assumptions and the wage equation are at the start of the appendix.
:::

## Young women remaining NEET cost about UAH `r CH("nat_year_c", 0)` billion a year {.smaller}
```{r c2, results='asis'}
FIG("c2_cost_of_inaction_national_en.png", "80%")
```

::: {style="font-size:0.58em; color:#7a7a7a;"}
Central scenario, of which UAH `r CH("nat_fiscal_c", 1)` billion would reach the budget; UAH `r CH("nat_year_pess", 0)` to `r CH("nat_year_opt", 0)` billion across scenarios. About `r CHK("n_neet_nat")` women aged 18–24 are NEET in the areas covered by HSESS 2023/24 (weighted count, out of about `r CHK("pop_w1824")` women of that age). The figure excludes areas the survey could not cover and should be updated with an official 2026 population estimate when available.
:::

## How to read the cost of inaction {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Is there demand for these workers?**

::: {style="font-size:.62em; line-height:1.35;"}
- Employers report record shortages: 69% of industrial firms cited a lack of workers in May 2026 (IER monthly enterprise survey), and 78% of employers reported a shortage in 2026 (OLX Robota and European Business Association).
- Firms are raising wages to recruit and keep staff, and some are hiring women into occupations traditionally held by men.
- But demand is uneven: only 32% of businesses surveyed by the State Employment Service planned to hire in 2026, and unemployment is still high (about 15% in early 2026, Info Sapiens).
- So demand exists, but jobs have to be reachable for young mothers: location, hours, childcare and skills matter as much as the number of vacancies.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**What the estimate does and does not capture**

::: {style="font-size:.62em; line-height:1.35;"}
*Likely to understate the cost:* it counts only earnings and taxes; it leaves out effects on children, on young women's future careers (lost experience), on employers, and the wider economy; the pessimistic case counts only women already looking for work.

*Likely to overstate it:* it assumes jobs are available at the wage of employed women with the same education, age and location, that new workers do not displace others, and that NEET women would earn as much as employed women with the same profile.

*How to use it:* as the order of magnitude of what is at stake, with a range rather than a single number, and as the benchmark against which the cost of support services can be judged.
:::
:::
:::

## Per 1,000 NEET young women: UAH `r CH("year_per1000_c")` million a year {.smaller}
```{r c1, results='asis'}
FIG("c1_cost_of_inaction_scenarios_en.png", "86%")
```

::: {style="font-size:0.58em; color:#7a7a7a;"}
1,000 NEET young women correspond to about `r CH("young_per1000")` women aged 18–24. Central scenario, of which UAH `r CH("fiscal_per1000_c")` million would reach the budget. The pessimistic, central and optimistic scenarios (UAH `r CH("year_per1000_pess")`, `r CH("year_per1000_c")` and `r CH("year_per1000_opt")` million) combine the lowest, middle and highest values found in the surveys for the wage, the share who would work and the share of formal jobs; the labels under each bar show the values used. Per 100,000 women aged 18–24, the central cost is UAH `r CH("per100k_c", 1)` billion a year.
:::

## Over five years, UAH `r CH("pv_per1000_pess")` to `r CH("pv_per1000_opt")` million per 1,000 {.smaller}
```{r c3, results='asis'}
FIG("c3_cost_of_inaction_pv_en.png", "80%")
```

::: {style="font-size:0.58em; color:#7a7a7a;"}
Present value of five years at a 5% discount rate (UAH `r CH("pv_per1000_cent")` million in the central scenario); the horizon and discount rate are the same in all three scenarios, which differ only in the survey-based parameters. A woman who remains NEET to age 60 forgoes about UAH `r CHM("lifetime_pv")` million in earnings and the budget UAH `r CHM("lifetime_fiscal_pv")` million (present values, central wage).
:::

## Mothers are `r CH("share_mothers")`% of NEET young women {.smaller}
```{r c4, results='asis'}
FIG("c4_cost_by_group_en.png", "82%")
```

::: {style="font-size:0.58em; color:#7a7a7a;"}
MICS 2025/26, women aged 18–24. This describes who the NEET young women are: the share of them in each group. Groups overlap, and `r CH("share_any")`% belong to at least one of the first five, so not every NEET young woman has one of these characteristics. Mothers are the largest identifiable group, so support that works for young mothers addresses the largest part of the cost.
:::

# 5 · Investment options {.section-divider background-color="#00377C"}

## What employment gain would justify each service? {.smaller}
```{r c7, results='asis'}
FIG("c7_break_even_by_intervention_en.png", "96%")
```

::: {style="font-size:0.58em; color:#7a7a7a;"}
Blue: share of participants who must gain additional employment for three years to cover the cost. Costs use existing Ukrainian amounts: 3 to 6 months of the minimum wage (UAH 8,647) for first-job support and 12 to 24 months of the eYasla payment (UAH 8,000 a month) for childcare; the cost of employment services is an assumption. Pink: employment effects from evaluations in other countries (Card, Kluve and Weber 2018 for employment programmes; Berlinski and Galiani 2007 and Clark et al. 2019 for childcare). None of these evaluations comes from a country in conflict, so the pink ranges are indicative for Ukraine; sources and caveats are in the appendix.
:::

## Illustrative returns by type of service {.smaller}
```{r c5, results='asis'}
FIG("c5_interventions_en.png", "96%")
```

::: {style="font-size:0.58em; color:#7a7a7a;"}
Benefits per UAH of cost, from the least to the most favourable combination of cost and effect, for young women's earnings, government receipts and both. Same costs and evidence as the previous slide. Employment services need the smallest employment gains to pay for themselves and first-job support gains close to those found in evaluations; childcare support at the level of the eYasla payment needs larger or longer-lasting gains to pay for itself through earnings and receipts alone. Benefits to children and employers are not counted.
:::

# 6 · Conclusions and recommendations {.section-divider background-color="#00377C"}

## Key messages {.smaller .bigtitle}

::: {.vmid-s}
::: {.kf-list style="font-size:.84em;"}
**1. The problem is large.** `r MH("neet_w_1824")`% of women aged 18–24 are NEET (MICS 2025/26); in HSESS, `r HS("st_neet_w")`% of women against `r HS("st_neet_m")`% of men.

**2. The gap is about education, not employment.** Young women and men work at the same rate (`r HS("st_emp_w")`% and `r HS("st_emp_m")`%); fewer women stay in education (`r HS("st_educ_w")`% against `r HS("st_educ_m")`%).

**3. Motherhood is the main factor.** NEET is `r GH("g1_mother_yes")`% among young mothers against `r GH("g1_mother_no")`% among other young women, and the difference remains after adjusting for other characteristics.

**4. Poverty compounds it.** Among poor young mothers NEET reaches `r GH("g4_mics_poor_mother")`% to `r GH("g4_hsess_poor_mother")`%; displacement is not associated with higher NEET.

**5. Inaction is costly.** Young women remaining NEET cost about UAH `r CH("nat_year_c", 0)` billion a year (range UAH `r CH("nat_year_pess", 0)` to `r CH("nat_year_opt", 0)` billion), of which UAH `r CH("nat_fiscal_c", 1)` billion would reach the budget.

**6. Services differ widely in cost.** Employment services need small employment gains to pay for themselves; first-job support needs gains close to those found in evaluations; childcare support needs the largest.
:::
:::

## Priority 1: Learning-to-Earning (First Experience, Earning Engine) {.smaller}

::: {.kv-table}
| Finding | Recommendation, building on existing mechanisms | Who | What the model indicates |
|---|---|---|---|
| At 18–24, young women and men are employed at the same rate; the NEET gap (`r HS("st_neet_w")`% against `r HS("st_neet_m")`%) mirrors lower education participation (`r HS("st_educ_w")`% against `r HS("st_educ_m")`%) | Support young women to stay in education and training, and bridge the exit with first work experience (internships, apprenticeships, first-job support) through the State Employment Service and employers | Ministry of Economy; State Employment Service; employers; education and VET institutions; UNICEF (GenU) | The employment gain first-job support needs to cover its cost is of the same order as the effects found in evaluations; shorter subsidies pay off more easily |
| NEET is lower with tertiary education (`r GH("tert_neet_w")`% against `r GH("vet_neet_w")`% vocational and `r GH("sec_neet_w")`% secondary, women 18–29); the vocational gap against secondary disappears once motherhood and area are accounted for | Do not treat vocational education as the cause: focus on the transition after it, especially for young mothers and rural women, and on guidance towards fields with employer demand | Ministry of Education and Science; VET institutions; State Employment Service; employers | Needs vacancy, pay and entry-requirement data by occupation (SES dashboard, SSSU) |
| Women earn less than men at every level of education (median wage gap at 18–24: `r HS("gap_1824")`%), although informal work is less common among women (`r HS("inf_w")`% against `r HS("inf_m")`%) | Pair first-job pathways with formal contracts and decent-work standards; monitor the pay gap by occupation | Employers; State Labour Service; State Employment Service | Each formal job adds about UAH `r CH("fiscal_year_c")` a year to the budget |
:::

## Priority 2: Inclusive Access and Navigation (protection and employment) {.smaller}

::: {.kv-table}
| Finding | Recommendation, building on existing mechanisms | Who | What the model indicates |
|---|---|---|---|
| Motherhood is the main factor: NEET is `r GH("g1_mother_yes")`% among young mothers against `r GH("g1_mother_no")`%, and mothers are `r CH("share_mothers")`% of NEET young women | Build on eYasla (UAH 8,000 a month for parents who return to full-time work): combine it with flexible working arrangements and family-friendly workplace policies, and give young mothers priority in employment services | Ministry of Social Policy, Family and National Unity; local authorities; employers; UNICEF | Childcare support is the most expensive option: it pays for itself through earnings and receipts only if a large share of supported mothers would not have worked otherwise, or if their employment lasts longer than three years |
| Poverty compounds it: NEET is `r GH("g1_poor20_yes")`% in the poorest fifth against `r GH("g1_poor20_no")`%, and `r GH("g4_mics_poor_mother")`% to `r GH("g4_hsess_poor_mother")`% among poor young mothers; it is also higher in single-headed households (`r GH("g2_single_yes_w")`% against `r GH("g2_single_no_w")`% in HSESS) | Link social assistance for low-income and single-headed households with employment services (referrals, case management), so that benefits and job support reach the same young women | Ministry of Social Policy; State Employment Service; hromadas | Existing benefit registries can identify most poor young mothers |
| Displacement is not associated with higher NEET (`r GH("g1_idp_yes")`% against `r GH("g1_idp_no")`%); disability groups are too small to estimate | Keep inclusive outreach through existing services for displaced young women and young women with disabilities, without a separate programme stream | Hromadas; IDP councils; UNICEF and partners | Not estimated; track outcomes as programmes report |
:::

# Appendix {.section-divider background-color="#00377C"}

## Cost of inaction: key assumptions {.smaller}

::: {.kv-table}
| Element | Assumption | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Population | NEET women aged 18–24: `r CH("neet_w", 1)`% (MICS). National total: weighted count of NEET women aged 18–24 in HSESS (about `r CHK("n_neet_nat")`). Per 1,000 NEET young women = about `r CH("young_per1000")` women aged 18–24 | MICS 2025/26; HSESS 2023/24 weights; override with an official 2026 estimate in COI$pop_w1824 |
| Potential earnings | Central: wage predicted for each NEET young woman by the wage equation on the next slide (UAH `r CH("wage_cent")` a month on average, n = `r CH("n_neet_pred")`). Bounds: 25th percentile and median wage of employed women aged 18–24 (n = `r CH("n_wage")`) | HSESS 2023/24; nominal UAH, Dec 2023 to Feb 2024 prices; no wage growth |
| Counterfactual | Zero earnings while NEET | Assumption |
| Share who could work | Already looking for work: `r CH("share_seeking")`%. Closing the gap with young men (`r CH("neet_w_h", 1)`% against `r CH("neet_m_h", 1)`%): `r CH("share_gap")`%. Looking for work or out of work because of care duties: `r CH("share_care_plus")`% | HSESS 2023/24 |
| Formal jobs | Formal share among employed women aged 18–24: `r CH("formal_low")`% without tertiary education, `r CH("formal_all")`% overall, `r CH("formal_high")`% with tertiary education | HSESS 2023/24 |
| Government receipts | 18% income tax and 5% military levy on the gross wage; 22% employer social contribution; 20% VAT on 80% of net earnings (consumption share assumed) | Statutory rates |
| Time | Annual cost; present value over 5 years at a 5% social discount rate; lifetime to age 60 | Same discount rate as A Brighter Future (UNICEF Ukraine, 2024) |
| Labour demand | Jobs assumed available at the wage of employed women with the same profile; no displacement of other workers | Assumption; employer surveys report shortages (see main deck) |
| Not included | Employer returns; women's work-related expenses; effects on children and other household members; wider economic effects | |
:::

## Wage equation behind the cost of inaction {.smaller}

::: {.eq-wrap}
::: {.eq-card}
[Step 1 · Estimation on employed women]{.eq-label}

::: {.eq}
ln <i>w</i><sub><i>i</i></sub> = α + Σ<sub><i>k</i></sub> β<sub><i>k</i></sub> Educ<sub><i>ik</i></sub> + γ<sub>1</sub> Age<sub><i>i</i></sub> + γ<sub>2</sub> Age<sub><i>i</i></sub><sup>2</sup> + δ Rural<sub><i>i</i></sub> + μ<sub>oblast(<i>i</i>)</sub> + ε<sub><i>i</i></sub>
:::

::: {.eq-note}
<i>w</i><sub><i>i</i></sub>: monthly net wage of employed woman <i>i</i> · Educ<sub><i>ik</i></sub>: highest level completed (reference: basic secondary or less) · μ: oblast effects
:::
:::

::: {.eq-card .pink}
[Step 2 · Prediction for each NEET young woman]{.eq-label}

::: {.eq}
ŵ<sub><i>j</i></sub> = exp( <i>x</i><sub><i>j</i></sub>′ β̂ ) × <i>S</i>, &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; <i>S</i> = Σ<sub><i>i</i></sub> ω<sub><i>i</i></sub> exp( ε̂<sub><i>i</i></sub> ) / Σ<sub><i>i</i></sub> ω<sub><i>i</i></sub>
:::

::: {.eq-note}
<i>x</i><sub><i>j</i></sub>: her own education level, age, area and oblast · <i>S</i>: smearing factor that converts predicted log wages back to UAH · ω<sub><i>i</i></sub>: survey weights
:::
:::

::: {.eq-grid}
<div><b>Sample</b><br>Employed women aged 18–64 with a reported wage, HSESS 2023/24: n = `r CH("n_mincer")`, R² = `r CH("r2_mincer", 2)`. Predictions for `r CH("n_neet_pred")` NEET women aged 18–24.</div>
<div><b>Estimation</b><br>Weighted least squares with survey weights. Coefficients in the next appendix slide.</div>
<div><b>Limits</b><br>No adjustment for hours, occupation or sector, and no correction for selection into work: NEET women may earn less than employed women with the same profile.</div>
:::
:::

## Wage equations behind the education and gender results {.smaller}

::: {.eq-wrap}
::: {.eq-card}
[Returns to a year of education · estimated separately for women and men]{.eq-label}

::: {.eq}
ln <i>w</i><sub><i>i</i></sub> = α + ρ <i>S</i><sub><i>i</i></sub> + γ<sub>1</sub> Age<sub><i>i</i></sub> + γ<sub>2</sub> Age<sub><i>i</i></sub><sup>2</sup> + μ<sub>oblast(<i>i</i>)</sub> + ε<sub><i>i</i></sub>
:::

::: {.eq-note}
<i>S</i><sub><i>i</i></sub>: years of education implied by the highest level completed (9, 11, 12, 13, 15 or 17) · Return per year = exp(ρ) − 1: `r MM("ret_w")`% for women, `r MM("ret_m")`% for men · Wage earners aged 18–64 · Standard errors clustered by household
:::
:::

::: {.eq-card .pink}
[Wages by education level and sex · women and men pooled]{.eq-label}

::: {.eq .long}
ln <i>w</i><sub><i>i</i></sub> = α + Σ<sub><i>k</i></sub> β<sub><i>k</i></sub> Educ<sub><i>ik</i></sub> + λ Woman<sub><i>i</i></sub> + Σ<sub><i>k</i></sub> θ<sub><i>k</i></sub> (Educ<sub><i>ik</i></sub> × Woman<sub><i>i</i></sub>) + γ<sub>1</sub> Age<sub><i>i</i></sub> + γ<sub>2</sub> Age<sub><i>i</i></sub><sup>2</sup> + δ Rural<sub><i>i</i></sub> + μ<sub>oblast(<i>i</i>)</sub> + ε<sub><i>i</i></sub>
:::

::: {.eq-note}
Adjusted gap at education level <i>k</i> = 1 − exp(λ + θ<sub><i>k</i></sub>), shown at age 30 in an urban area · Wage earners aged 18–64 · Neither equation adjusts for hours, occupation or sector, or for selection into work
:::
:::
:::

## Investment options: sources for costs and employment effects {.smaller}

::: {.kv-small}
```{r srctab}
if (!is.null(.src)) kable(.src)
```
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.55em; color:#7a7a7a;"}
Card, Kluve and Weber (2018), Journal of the European Economic Association 16(3); Berlinski and Galiani (2007), Labour Economics 14; Clark, Kabiru, Laszlo and Muthuri (2019), Demography 56; Halim, Perova and Reynolds (2023), World Bank Research Observer 38(1). None of these evaluations comes from a country in conflict. In Ukraine, labour shortages could make effects larger, while safety, displacement and childcare closures could make them smaller; Card, Kluve and Weber find larger effects for women and in weak labour markets. The ranges should be replaced with Ukrainian evidence, for example State Employment Service follow-up data, when available.
:::

## Evidence on employment effects (1/2): employment programmes {.smaller}

::: {.kv-table}
| Study | Where and when | Design | What was tested | Effect on employment | Comparability with Ukraine |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Card, Kluve and Weber (2018)**, Journal of the European Economic Association | 207 evaluations, 857 estimates, 47 countries; mostly European and other high-income countries | Meta-analysis of impact evaluations (experimental and non-experimental) | Training, job search assistance, subsidised employment, public works | +1.6 pp within a year; +5.4 pp after one to two years; +8.7 pp after two years | Not specific to youth. Medium- and long-run effects are similar in high- and middle-income countries; effects are larger for women and in weak labour markets. Used for the employment services and first-job ranges |
| **Kluve et al. (2019)**, World Development | 113 evaluations of 107 youth programmes in 31 countries | Meta-analysis of youth employment programmes | Training, entrepreneurship, employment services, subsidised employment | Small on average; about one third of estimates positive and significant; employment services and subsidised employment small and often not significant | Specific to youth. Larger effects in low- and middle-income countries, for disadvantaged youth, and for programmes combining several services. Suggests the upper ranges for employment services alone may be optimistic |
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.55em; color:#7a7a7a;"}
No published impact evaluation of a State Employment Service programme for young women in Ukraine was found. None of the studies comes from a country in conflict.
:::

## Evidence on employment effects (2/2): childcare {.smaller}

::: {.kv-table}
| Study | Where and when | Design | What was tested | Effect on employment | Comparability with Ukraine |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Berlinski and Galiani (2007)**, Labour Economics | Argentina, national expansion of public preschool places in the 1990s | Natural experiment: timing of new preschool places across areas | Free public preschool for children aged 3 to 5 | Maternal employment +7 to +14 pp | Middle-income country with formal labour markets. Places for children aged 3 to 5, while eYasla is a cash payment for children aged 1 to 3 |
| **Clark, Kabiru, Laszlo and Muthuri (2019)**, Demography | Kenya, informal settlement in Nairobi, from 2015 | Randomised controlled trial | Vouchers for subsidised early childcare | +8.5 pp for mothers offered vouchers (about +20 pp among those who used the care); gains mostly among married mothers | Closest in mechanism to eYasla (a subsidy that mothers choose how to use), but low-income setting with mostly informal work |
| **Halim, Perova and Reynolds (2023)**, World Bank Research Observer | 22 studies in low- and middle-income countries | Review of studies with credible causal designs | Public childcare, longer care hours, lower childcare costs | Positive in all but one study | Confirms the direction of the effect across very different settings; no single effect size |
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.55em; color:#7a7a7a;"}
eYasla started in January 2026 and could be evaluated directly, for example by comparing employment of eligible mothers before and after it started or across eligibility thresholds; that would replace these ranges with Ukrainian evidence.
:::

## How this builds on earlier investment cases {.smaller}

::: {.vmid-s}
::: {.tight-table}
| | A Brighter Future (UNICEF Ukraine, 2024) | This analysis |
|---|---|---|
| **Focus** | Early childhood development: children under six | Young women aged 18–24 who are not in education, employment or training |
| **Question** | Returns to scaling up childcare, preschool, health, social protection and WASH services to 2050 | Who is excluded, why, what it costs each year, and what employment gain would justify each service |
| **Data** | National statistics, mostly from before 2022, and regional assumptions | Microdata collected since 2022: MICS 2025/26 and HSESS 2023/24 |
| **Link** | Estimates that expanding childcare would allow caregivers, mainly women, to return to work | Measures that link directly: motherhood and childcare are the main reasons young women are out of work |
:::
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.58em; color:#7a7a7a;"}
The two are complementary: the earlier case argues for expanding early childhood services; this one identifies the young women who would use them and what their exclusion costs. Both use a 5% social discount rate.
:::

## How the intervention parameters are built and updated {.smaller}

::: {.kv-table}
| Step | What was done | How the country office can update it |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Intervention types | Four types from the GenU priorities: employment services (counselling and job matching), employer-supported internships and first jobs, childcare services with flexible work, and a combined package for young mothers | Add rows to code/intervention_parameters.csv (one per intervention or package), with a target group |
| 2. Costs | Present value of the total cost per participant over the support period, low and high, from existing Ukrainian programme amounts where available | Replace with State Employment Service, partner and UNICEF unit costs |
| 3. Employment effects | Additional, sustained employment attributable to the intervention, low and high, from published evaluations in other countries (sources on the previous slide) | Replace with Ukrainian evaluations where available (for example SES programme follow-up data) |
| 4. Benefits | Effect multiplied by the annual value of a job (net earnings; income tax, levy, contributions and VAT) over the years sustained, discounted at 5% | Change wage, formality or duration in 04_cost_of_inaction.R to test scenarios |
| 5. Outputs | Benefit-cost ratios by perspective, break-even employment gains, and the comparison with the evidence range | Re-run bash UPDATE_RESULTS.sh; all slides update |
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.55em; color:#7a7a7a;"}
Employer returns (productivity, retention, vacancy costs) are not included and would be the next step for the private sector case.
:::

## Age groups {.smaller}

::: {.vmid-s}
::: {.tight-table}
| Age group | Used for | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **18–24** | Main group: NEET, employment, earnings, cost of inaction | In line with government statistics and UNICEF programming |
| **15–17** | NEET and employment among the younger group | MICS asks the NEET questions to women aged 15–24; HSESS asks employment questions from age 15 |
| **14–17** | School attendance | Available for all household members in both surveys |

MICS 2025/26 has no men's questionnaire, so NEET and employment in MICS refer to women; comparisons between women and men use HSESS 2023/24 and, for school attendance, the MICS household roster.
:::

## Variables and definitions (1/2) {.smaller}

::: {.kv-table}
| Concept | Definition | MICS 2025/26 | HSESS 2023/24 | LFS 2021 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **In education** | Attending school or university in the current school year | ED9 (members 3–24); NE3 (women 15–24) | IND_A9 | reason_inactiv = 2 (inactive students) |
| **Employed** | Worked at least one hour for pay or profit in the reference week, or temporarily absent; production for own household use only is not counted | NE8–NE11, NE20–NE21 (women 15–24) | IND_B1 | labour_force = 1 |
| **NEET** | Not in education or training and not employed | NEET module (women 15–24) | IND_A9, IND_B1 | labour_force, reason_inactiv (upper bound) |
| **Labour-force participation** | Employed, or looking for work or starting a business | not available | IND_B1, IND_B21 | labour_force 1–2 |
| **Informal employment** | Verbal agreement, unregistered own-account work, or family farm work for sale | not available | IND_B3_1 | informal_empl = 1 |
| **Mother** | Has given birth (MICS) or lives with own child under 18 (HSESS) | CEB | household roster (IND_A1, ages) | not available |
:::

## Variables and definitions (2/2) {.smaller}

::: {.kv-table}
| Concept | Definition | MICS 2025/26 | HSESS 2023/24 | LFS 2021 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Care work** | Caring for children or the sick in the past week (5–17); daily care of own children | CL11E, CL11F | IND_B28_1 | reason_inactiv = 3 (proxy) |
| **Internally displaced** | Self-reported IDP status | WB10A | IND_A19 | not available |
| **Disability** | Washington Group functional difficulty (18–49); any household member with disability | AF module | D1_Mult3/4 | not available |
| **Economic status** | Wealth quintile; household income per member | windex5 | V1 / household size | not available |
| **Years of education** | Years implied by the highest level completed (9 basic secondary, 11 complete secondary, 12 vocational, 13 short-cycle, 15 bachelor, 17 master) | welevel | IND_A7 | education |
:::

## HSESS variables used {.smaller}

::: {.kv-small}
```{r hvars}
hv <- .rdc("tables/hsess_variables_used.csv")
if (!is.null(hv)) {
  hv <- hv %>% filter(!is.na(code)) %>%
    mutate(code = case_when(role == "key" ~ "questionnaire key", role == "weight" ~ "final weight",
                            grepl("[^ -~]", code) ~ role, TRUE ~ code),
           v = paste0(role, " (", ifelse(file == "individual", "ind", "hh"), ")"))
  k <- ceiling(nrow(hv) / 3); pad <- function(x) c(x, rep("", 3 * k - length(x)))
  v <- pad(hv$v); cd <- pad(hv$code); i <- function(j) ((j - 1) * k + 1):(j * k)
  kable(data.frame(v[i(1)], cd[i(1)], v[i(2)], cd[i(2)], v[i(3)], cd[i(3)]), col.names = rep(c("Variable", "Code"), 3))
}
```
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.55em; color:#7a7a7a;"}
Codes as in the questionnaire and the "variables_ukr" sheet of each HSESS file; "ind" = individual file, "hh" = household file.
:::
